name: normalized-heterogeneous-ast
intent: Represent an abstract syntax tree with several node types that each carry their own data while every node exposes the same normalized child-list accessor, so one generic walker, visitor or tree matcher can traverse any subtree without knowing node-specific fields.
problem: A language tool needs node-specific data (a binary operator's symbol, an if-statement's condition and branches, a literal's value) but its passes - printing, name resolution, type checking, rewriting, serialisation, tree matching - operate on arbitrary subtrees. If each node keeps its children only in node-specific named fields, every pass must enumerate and understand every node type, so each new node type or field ripples through all existing passes; if all nodes are collapsed into one generic node shape, node-specific data is lost and the difference between an if's condition and its body becomes a positional convention.
context: Hand-written parsers, interpreters, compilers, linters and DSL tools whose node set is closed and known at compile time and which are consumed by several generic passes rather than by node-local operations. It is the natural choice when external tree visitors, structural rewrites or tree pattern matchers must work over arbitrary subtrees, and it is what most maintained AST libraries (Go's go/ast, CPython's ast, Roslyn, ESTree producers) actually do.
benefits: One walker, visitor, printer, serialiser or tree matcher serves every node type: generic passes recurse over the normalized children collection instead of enumerating node types.
Node-specific data stays fully typed on the concrete node (operator token, literal value, computed type), so the heterogeneity is not flattened into a property bag.
Adding an analysis touches no node type: new passes reuse the child protocol, which is why Parr recommends this shape together with an external tree visitor (Pattern 13).
New node types stay cheap to add as long as their constructor registers their children, keeping the parser's grammar and the tree's types in step.
The traversal contract is testable in one place: a single dump or printer renders any node, and one invariant checks that every node's children are reachable.
Structural rewriting and matching operate on shapes rather than on hand-written per-type traversal code.
tradeoffs: The child list is maintained by hand in every node constructor: a node that forgets to append a child silently disappears from every generic pass, and no type checker catches it.

Children are positional, so roles are lost to generic passes: code that needs 'the condition' or 'the target' re-derives it by index or by a cast, which is exactly the knowledge the node-specific fields encode.
Node-specific methods and embedded walkers become awkward (Parr points such code at the irregular AST): per-node behaviour has no shared traversal hook unless one is added to the base.
Uniform child access invites over-general passes that recurse into token, comment and annotation slots, which is cheap to write and expensive to run.

Trees are graphs of separately allocated nodes with an indirection per child (pointers, unique_ptr, Box/Rc): deep trees pay allocation and recursion-depth costs, and sharing or accidental cycles become possible.
Nothing in the type system prevents a child being stored twice - once in a named field and once in the child list - so clone, rewrite and serialisation code must uphold that invariant explicitly.

participants.responsibility: Concrete representation of one grammar alternative: a heterogeneous type carrying node-specific data (operator token, literal value, computed type) in addition to its children.
The uniform, positional collection of child nodes that every node exposes; the single traversal contract of the pattern.
Base class or interface that owns or declares the normalized child-list protocol (children(), child_nodes, ChildNodes()) plus any cross-cutting payload such as a source span or node kind.
Method or iterator through which a walker obtains a node's children (accessor, accept/visit pair) without knowing the concrete type.
Traversal, printing, matching or rewriting code that recurses through the protocol and works on any subtree, including node types added later.
Construction side: instantiate the concrete node and append its children to the normalized list in the canonical order.

use_cases: Compilers and interpreters for a small language or DSL whose tree is consumed by several generic passes (printing, resolution, type checks, optimisation, code generation).
Tree pattern matchers and rewriting engines that match or replace arbitrary subtree shapes and therefore need every node's children through one accessor.
Linters, formatters and refactoring tools that walk arbitrary nodes and must not enumerate every node type in every rule.
AST libraries and toolchains whose nodes expose a uniform child contract so third-party tools can traverse trees they do not own (go/ast, CPython ast, Roslyn SyntaxNode, ESTree).
Tree serialisation, diffing and pretty-printing where one generic renderer must handle every node kind.
Language servers and IDE tooling that index a whole tree by recursively collecting children.

Python's ast module supports generic analysis and rewriting over heterogeneous nodes: NodeVisitor and NodeTransformer use generic_visit, while iter_child_nodes exposes direct children to custom passes.
Go source tooling walks typed go/ast nodes with ast.Inspect or ast.Walk, using depth-first traversal and callback-controlled descent without each pass reimplementing child enumeration.
Roslyn analyzers traverse SyntaxNode.ChildNodes or DescendantNodes, while ESTree-compatible JavaScript tools consume standardized heterogeneous node shapes through shared traversal tooling.
avoid_when: Node-specific operations dominate and generic traversal is rare: named child fields on per-node types (the irregular heterogeneous AST) read better and catch role mistakes at compile time.
The tree is uniform or data-driven (JSON/XML-style documents, generic expression trees): one node type with a child list or map is simpler than a family of types.
A maintained AST library already provides the tree for the syntax you target (Go's go/ast, CPython ast, Roslyn, ESTree producers): reuse its node types instead of hand-rolling a second tree.
A single hand-written pass walks the tree exactly once (interpret while parsing, streaming transform): no shared traversal contract is needed, so the child-list discipline buys nothing.

Child roles and arity must be enforced by the type system (a typed IR where a wrong child must be a compile error): named fields or an algebraic data type express that invariant; a positional list does not.
anti_patterns: A 'normalized' tree whose nodes append children ad hoc, so generic passes quietly skip subtrees the constructor forgot - the exact failure the pattern exists to prevent.
Exposing the mutable child list publicly, letting any pass splice children into the tree and invalidate every traversal and cache built on it.
Re-deriving node roles by index everywhere (children[0] is the callee, children[1] the first argument), discarding the node-specific data the types already carry.
Re-implementing a normalized AST on top of a library that already provides one (Roslyn, go/ast, CPython ast, ESTree) and converting between the two representations at every boundary.
Giving the base class every possible slot (children, tokens, trivia, annotations, comments) and letting walkers recurse into all of them, so generic traversal becomes the slow path.
design_principles: Uniform interface over heterogeneous data: the child-access protocol is the one thing every node type shares, and it is what generic code depends on.
Separation of representation from traversal: nodes own their data and the child list; walking, matching and rewriting live outside the node types.
Open/closed at the operation level: new passes reuse the child protocol without modifying node types.
Liskov substitutability under the traversal contract: any node can appear anywhere the base type is expected and must yield its children correctly.
Single source of truth for the child collection: exactly one place per node determines which children exist and in what order.
best_practices: Give the base type the only child-storage implementation so every node stores children identically and one accessor serves all traversals.
Append children in the concrete constructor in a documented canonical order; treat that order as part of the node's contract and test it with a canonical dump.
Keep payload out of the child list: tokens, spans and computed types are node data, not children, or generic passes will start walking them.
Expose children read-only (immutable list, span or iterator) and finish building the tree before any pass runs.
Provide exactly one generic traversal entry point (walk/visit/inspect) plus the per-node dispatch mechanism, and make new node types check both.
Test with a golden serialisation of the whole tree: a uniform renderer makes a missing child visible immediately.
Keep an escape hatch for node-specific operations instead of forcing every analysis through the child protocol.
sources: Parr, Language Implementation Patterns: Create Your Own Domain-Specific and General Programming Languages (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2010) - Pattern 10, Normalized Heterogeneous AST (ch. 4, Building Abstract Syntax Trees), pp. 113-115: more than one node data type while retaining the normalized child list, recommended when nodes carry specific data and an external tree visitor (Pattern 13) will be used; heavy per-node methods or an embedded walker (Pattern 12) instead favour Pattern 11, Irregular Heterogeneous AST.
